summary: A survey of which hosts accept connections for Telnet, FTP and mail over TCP, this edition run in February 1983. It continues a series by David Smallberg. Replaced by RFC 846.

eli5.summary: Someone knocked on every computer's door to see which would answer. This is one week's tally.

subtitle: A host connectivity snapshot from February 1983.

tldr.problem: Network engineers needed to know which hosts could actually speak TCP and offer services like Telnet, FTP and SMTP. Without this information, connection failures were difficult to debug.
tldr.mechanism: David Smallberg ran automated tests from February 15-17, 1983, connecting to every host in the NIC hostname table and testing whether it accepted Telnet, FTP and SMTP connections.
tldr.outcome: Out of 329 hosts tested, 176 accepted Telnet, 169 accepted FTP, and 157 accepted SMTP. Many claimed TCP support but did not actually accept connections. This survey is Historic, replaced by RFC 846.

today: RFC 845 is a historical survey and has been superseded by RFC 846, the March 1983 edition of the same survey. While both are now historic documents, they provide valuable snapshots of early TCP adoption and network reliability, showing the state of the Internet as it was transitioning from the ARPANET era.

sections.title: The Survey
sections.content:
RFC 845 reports the results of a survey of which Internet hosts accept TCP connections for three key services: Telnet, FTP (File Transfer Protocol), and SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol). The survey was conducted by David Smallberg in February 1983, run from ISI-VAXA.ARPA.

The test hosts came from the NIC hostname table as of February 3, 1983. Tests were run on February 15 from 8 am to 12:30 pm PST, then on February 16 from 10 am to 11:10 am PST. Hosts that did not respond were retried from 10 pm February 16 to 6:40 am February 17. This survey continues a series of similar reports showing the state of TCP deployment in the network.

The results show a snapshot of the Internet at a moment in time when TCP was still being deployed. Many hosts either did not implement TCP or did not offer the tested services.
sections.eli5: Someone dialed every computer's number and tried to reach it on three different services: Telnet, FTP, and mail. This RFC records who answered during one week in February 1983.

sections.title: Test Methodology
sections.content:
The survey was conducted by attempting connections to every host in the NIC hostname table. For each host, the test checked whether it claimed to support TCP and then tried to actually accept connections on the three services.

Claims were taken from the NIC host table using a simple notation: T meant TCP (no particular service), t meant TCP/Telnet support, f meant TCP/FTP support, and s meant TCP/SMTP support. A dash meant no claim for that service.

Each service test reported one of six results: blank (connection not accepted), refused (host actively refused the connection), unreachable (packets could not reach the host), dead (host did not respond at all), accepted (host accepted the connection normally), or accepted+ (the service had additional features, such as FTP allowing anonymous login with password guest).
sections.eli5: The test checked what each host claimed it could do, then tried to connect on three services. For each, the test noted whether the connection worked, was refused, timed out, or the host was dead.

sections.title: Summary Results
sections.content:
Out of 329 hosts tested, summary statistics showed significant variation between claimed capabilities and actual behavior.

For Telnet: 217 hosts claimed Telnet support, of which 155 actually accepted connections. The remaining 62 either did not respond (31 dead), were unreachable (10), refused (5), or did not implement Telnet despite claiming support (16). 112 hosts made no Telnet claim but 12 still accepted Telnet connections anyway.

For FTP: 199 hosts claimed FTP support, with 144 actually accepting connections. 28 claimed FTP but were dead, 10 were unreachable, 4 refused, and 13 claimed but did not accept. 111 hosts made no FTP claim; 16 of those still accepted FTP anyway.

For SMTP: 181 hosts claimed SMTP support, with only 124 accepting mail connections. 35 were dead, 10 were unreachable, 9 refused, and 10 claimed but did not accept. 129 hosts made no SMTP claim; 25 of those still accepted mail.
sections.eli5: Of 329 computers tested, most that claimed to do Telnet actually did (155 of 217 claims). But for mail, only 68 percent worked (124 of 181). Many dead hosts made no claims at all.

sections.title: Host Findings and Patterns
sections.content:
The survey included diverse systems across the early Internet, including major research institutions, military networks, and emerging universities. Each host had an IP address and a name, with claims and test results for each service.

Some patterns emerged: hosts that were dead or unreachable had failed across all services. Hosts that accepted one service usually accepted the others, though some accepted FTP but refused Telnet. A few hosts (like those with addresses in class 4, the Satellite Network, SATNET) were unreachable, suggesting link or routing failures.

The results highlight the early state of TCP adoption: many hosts did not implement these protocols, implementations were sometimes inconsistent, and some systems claimed capability they did not actually provide. The distinction between claimed and actual capability underscores the value of empirical testing in an evolving network.

The raw data lists results in two orders: alphabetical by hostname, then by IP address order, allowing readers to look up specific hosts or browse by network.
sections.eli5: Some computers worked for all three services. Others were broken or unreachable. A few claimed they did something but actually didn't. The data shows the network was still rough around the edges.
